title: Variables in Python
summary: Introduce assignment, naming, and the REPL feedback cycle.

checkpoints.title: Why variables?
checkpoints.content: Variables store references to objects. Python binds names to values at runtime.
checkpoints.explanation: Use variables to avoid repeating literal values and to communicate intent.

hints.H0: Scan the sample REPL transcript and notice the arrow prompt.
hints.H1: Look at how the same number is reused after assigning it a name.
hints.H2: Names let you change one assignment instead of many literals.

checkpoints.title: Complete an assignment
checkpoints.content: Complete the assignment so that the name `level` stores the result of `score + 1`.
checkpoints.explanation: Assignment uses a single equals sign to bind the expression's value to the name on the left.

hints.H0: Start by writing the name that should receive the value.
hints.H1: Remember Python evaluates the right-hand expression before binding.

checkpoints.title: Predict reassignment
checkpoints.content: After running `coins = 3` and then `coins = coins + 2`, what does `coins` hold?

options.text: It stays at 3 because the original value is preserved.
options.explanation: Reassignment updates the name to point at the new result.

options.text: It becomes 5, the result of the expression.
options.explanation: `coins + 2` evaluates to 5, and that value is bound back to `coins`.

options.text: It raises a NameError because coins is reused.
options.explanation: Names can be reused—Python simply updates the reference.

checkpoints.explanation: The second line rebinds `coins` to the new integer value produced by the expression.

hints.H0: Think about what `coins + 2` evaluates to given the current value.
hints.H1: When the expression runs, Python creates a new integer.
